The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we explain the idea of the proof of Theorem 1 and describe the methods we use. In Section 3 we give a brief overview of the theory of modular forms. In Section 4 we construct supplementary radial functions
, which are eigenfunctions of the Fourier transform and have double zeroes at
. This construction is crucial for our proof of Theorem 1. Finally, in Section 5 we complete the proof.

Our proof of Theorem 1 is based on linear programming bounds. This technique was successfully applied to obtain upper bounds in a wide range of discrete optimization problems such as error-correcting codes [7], equal weight quadrature formulas [8], and spherical codes [13, 16]. In exceptional cases linear programming bounds are optimal [5]. However, in general linear programming bounds are not sharp and it is an open question how big the errors of such bounds can be. It is known [2] that the linear programming bounds for the minimal number of points in an equal weight quadrature formula on the sphere
are asymptotically optimal up to a constant depending on
Linear programming bounds can also be applied to the sphere packing problem. Kabatiansky and Levenshtein [13] deduced upper bounds for sphere packing from their results on spherical codes.

In 2003 Cohn and Elkies [4] developed linear programming bounds that apply directly to sphere packings. Using their new method they improved the previously known upper bounds for the sphere packing constant in dimensions from 4 to 36. The most striking results obtained by this technique are upper bounds for dimensions 8 and 24. For example, their upper bound for
was only 1.000001 times greater than the lower bound, which is given by the density of the
sphere packing. This bound can be improved even further by more extensive computer computations.
